name: Ian Bremmer
role: American political scientist, Eurasia Group founder and GZERO Media president
summary: Bremmer supports international cooperation, competitive enterprise and social protection for people excluded from economic gains. His policy recommendations emphasize climate coordination, AI governance and limits on executive power; he distinguishes his geopolitical forecasts from personal preferences.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Says he would happily pay more tax personally and through Eurasia Group if it bought equality of opportunity and infrastructure, but does not specify a rate; the statement is conditional.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Calls for technology companies to participate in binding international AI governance.

cut-welfare.rationale: Insists people disadvantaged by globalization need support and regrets prospective subsidy cuts.

strong-leader.rationale: Opposes executive attacks on constitutional restraints despite acknowledging some effective policies.

state-harmful.rationale: Treats effective public institutions and social protection as necessary.

limit-guns.rationale: Says he supports gun rights but also names Canada's reasonable gun control as a model; the sources pull in both directions.

decide-locally.rationale: Praises state-level decision-making as a source of American resilience.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Lists gay marriage among the liberties he says he supports, in his own column and on camera (2021).

gradual-change.rationale: Calls necessary political disruption an opportunity rather than something to fear.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Advocates stronger global institutions, including enforceable international digital governance.

free-trade.rationale: Defends globalization’s gains but explicitly recognizes lasting losers who require compensation; benefits are not universal.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Mixed: he earlier proposed major public climate investment, but more recently emphasizes energy innovation and says global climate governance is unnecessary.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Expresses optimism that new technology creates solutions faster than problems, while recognizing risks.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Includes nuclear expansion among necessary post-carbon energy solutions.

experts-over-public.rationale: Wants expert-directed AI governance insulated from politicians’ limited expertise and electoral time horizons.

basic-income.rationale: Discusses income support as an option but questions whether basic-income experiments improve democratic participation.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Rejects sweeping protective tariffs as economically damaging.

political-violence-never.rationale: Says political violence in all its forms is something a democracy cannot tolerate; stated of the US, not as a universal philosophy.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Insists rapid AI deployment requires safeguards and governance against catastrophic misuse.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Insists policies can succeed despite his rejection of the politician responsible; separates assessment from preference.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Says fiscal stimulus is right in recessions and that deficit spending that builds long-term assets (education, health, infrastructure, decarbonization) is fine, while urging tightening in booms.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Endorses boosting US oil and gas as a bridge fuel while investing in clean energy; says nothing on coal, so the answer is partial.

proportional-representation.rationale: Answering a question about multi-party proportional representation, says a multi-party system would be a constructive development, while doubting it can be achieved.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Calls American politics kleptocratic and dominated by money.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Advocates government responsibilities in social protection, research and climate policy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Explicitly denies that Americans have greater intrinsic worth than other people.

trade-surplus.rationale: Rejects treating bilateral deficits as proof that trade partners exploit America.

separated-powers.rationale: Wants an independent judiciary to constrain executive abuses.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Proposes shared digital rules, a permanent secretariat and international judicial enforcement.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Defends NATO’s value and criticizes policies undermining its coherence.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Calls on wealthy Japan to coordinate humanitarian assistance for people and governments in need.

collective-defense.rationale: Stresses Article 5, that allies answered it after 9/11, and says an Article 5-style tripwire is needed for deterrence; doubt over US commitment is a gift to Moscow.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Treats executive refusal to obey judicial rulings as a constitutional danger.

space-expansion.rationale: Prioritizes caring for people on Earth over business leaders’ ambitions for Mars.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Defends courts’ ability to restrain a popularly elected executive.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Says in his view President Trump should be removed from office (impeached) for weaponized disinformation about the election, favoring the constitutional route.

corporate-influence.rationale: Criticizes lobbying and privileged political access that let the wealthy buy opportunities.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Accepts creative destruction as an engine of growth while demanding protection for those harmed.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Condemns weaponizing justice, tax and investigative agencies against political enemies.

social-market-economy.rationale: Wants American growth combined with stronger European-style social protection.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Condemns combining immense private wealth, presidential patronage and public administrative power.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Makes preventing catastrophic AI-driven conflict a central reason for international governance.

notes:
Forecasts, interview questions, guests’ views and descriptions of voter attitudes are not treated as personal preferences. The 2019 climate-investment recommendation is qualified by the August 2026 emphasis on innovation rather than global climate governance. Political revolution refers to institutional transformation such as Roosevelt’s, not an endorsement of violence. Specific speech, religious and immigration policies remain unknown without direct evidence. All remaining null statements reviewed; no living-person inferences.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 9 answers taken from it, 12 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass, from his own words only: about 1,030 GZERO Media pages (his 'by Ian Bremmer' columns and Q&As, Quick Takes, Ask Ian, Ian Explains), downloaded and searched by theme, and 820 of his CNN/NPR interview turns 2001-2020 (MediaSum). Forecasts, analysis of what leaders will do and descriptions of what voters want were not counted as positions. Themes searched: economy (health, tax, minimum wage, deficits, trade, UBI), government (elections, courts, executive power, money in politics, term limits), world (NATO, UN, EU, intervention, Israel, China, sanctions, arms control), liberty (speech, guns, drugs, privacy, surveillance), society (abortion, marriage, immigration), ecology and technology. Marijuana support does not settle drugs generally; support for skilled immigration does not settle overall levels; his support for free speech and verified human accounts does not settle hate-speech law or anonymity; platform liability and privacy-law comments do not settle corporate regulation in general; AI-governance remarks do not settle existential-risk priority. Abortion, healthcare, minimum wage, basic income, death penalty, Israel and Taiwan: only analysis, no stated preference. His four books (J Curve, Free Market, Every Nation for Itself, Superpower, Us vs. Them) are lending-only on archive.org and were not available as text. No answer rests on what a government did rather than on his own words.
